questions.q:
Four statements are given (A is mass number) :
A. The volume of a nucleus is proportional to $A^{1/3}$.
B. The volume of a nucleus is proportional to $A$.
C. The difference in mass of an atom and its nucleus is called the mass defect.
D. The difference in mass of a nucleus and its constituents is called the mass defect.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: A and C are true, but B and D are false
B and C are true, but A and D are false
A and D are true, but B and C are false
B and D are true, but A and C are false
questions.solution:
The radius of a nucleus is given by $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$.

The volume of the nucleus is $V = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi R_0^3 A$.

Thus, the volume of a nucleus is directly proportional to its mass number $A$. Statement A is false and Statement B is true.

The mass defect is defined as the difference between the sum of the masses of the constituent nucleons (protons and neutrons) and the actual mass of the nucleus.

Thus, Statement C is false and Statement D is true.

Therefore, B and D are true, but A and C are false.

Answer: B and D are true, but A and C are false

questions.q:
Consider the following nuclear reaction :
$^{238}\text{U}\rightarrow{}^{234}\text{Th}+{}^4\text{He}$
Take masses of $^{238}\text{U}$, $^{234}\text{Th}$ and $^4\text{He}$ as $238.050$ u, $234.043$ u and $4.003$ u, respectively. The Q value for the reaction, in keV, is :
[Given : $1$ u $=931.5$ MeV c$^{-2}$]
questions.solution:
The mass defect $\Delta m$ for the given nuclear reaction is:

$\Delta m = m(^{238}\text{U}) - [m(^{234}\text{Th}) + m(^4\text{He})]$

$\Delta m = 238.050 - (234.043 + 4.003)$

$\Delta m = 238.050 - 238.046 = 0.004 \text{ u}$

The $Q$ value of the reaction is given by:

$Q = \Delta m \times 931.5 \text{ MeV}$

$Q = 0.004 \times 931.5 \text{ MeV}$

$Q = 3.726 \text{ MeV}$

Converting to keV:

$Q = 3.726 \times 10^3 \text{ keV} = 3726 \text{ keV}$

Answer: $3726$

questions.q: A nucleus ${ }^A_Z X$ has mass represented by $M(A, Z)$. If $M_p$ and $M_n$ denote the mass of proton and neutron respectively and B.E. the binding energy in $\mathrm{MeV}$, then
options: B. E. $=\left[Z M_p+(A-Z) M_n-M(A, Z)\right] c^2$
B. E. $=\left[Z M_p+A M_n-M(A, Z)\right] c^2$
B. E. $=\left[M(A, Z)-Z M_p-(A-Z) M_n\right] c^2$.
questions.solution:
In the case of formation of a nucleus the evolution of energy equal to the binding energy of the nucleus takes place due to disappearance of a fraction of the total mass. If the quantity of mass disappearing is \(\Delta \mathrm{M}\). then the binding energy is
\(\mathrm{BE}=\Delta \mathrm{Mc}^2\)
From the above discussion, it is clear that the mass of the nucleus must be less than the sum of the masses of the constituent neutrons and protons. We can then write
\(\Delta \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{ZM}_{\mathrm{p}}+\mathrm{NM}_{\mathrm{p}}-\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{Z})\)
Where \(M(A, Z)\) is the mass of the atom of mass number \(A\) and atomic number \(Z\). Hence, the binding energy of the nucleus is
\(\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{BE}=\left[\mathrm{ZM}_{\mathrm{p}}+\mathrm{NM}_{\mathrm{n}}-\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{Z})\right] \mathrm{c}^2 \\
& \mathrm{BE}=\left[\mathrm{ZM}_{\mathrm{p}}+(\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{Z}) \mathrm{M}_{\mathrm{n}}-\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{Z})\right] \mathrm{c}^2
\end{aligned}\)
Where \(N=A-Z=\) Number of neutrons.

questions.solution: The correct option is (A). Nuclear fusion requires extremely high temperatures because the reacting nuclei are positively charged and repel each other due to electrostatic forces. At very high temperatures, the kinetic energy of the nuclei becomes large enough to overcome this repulsion, allowing them to get close enough for the strong nuclear force to bind them together, leading to fusion.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
When a nucleus with atomic number Z and mass number A undergoes a radioactive decay process:
(A) both Z and A will decrease if the process is \(\alpha\) - decay
(B) Z will decrease but A will not change if process is \(\beta^{+}\)decay
(C) Z will decrease but A will not change if process is \(\beta^{-}\)decay.
(D) Z and A will remain unchanged if process is \(\gamma\)-decay.
Choose the correct statement :
questions.solution:
- (A) both Z and A will decrease if the process is a-decay: True. In a-decay, a nucleus emits an alpha particle (_2^4$He), so Z decreases by 2 and A decreases by 4.
- (B) \(\mathrm{Z}\) will decrease but \(A\) will not change if process is \(\beta^{+}\)decay: True. In \(\beta^{+}\)decay (positron emission), a proton converts to a neutron, emitting a positron (_1^0$e). So Z decreases by 1, and A remains unchanged.
- (C) \(\mathrm{Z}\) will decrease but \(\mathrm{A}\) will not change if process is \(\beta\) - decay: False. In \(\beta\) - decay (electron emission), a neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron (\(_{-1}^{0} \mathrm{e}\)). So Z increases by 1, and A remains unchanged.
- (D) Z and A will remain unchanged if process is y-decay: True. Gamma decay involves the emission of a high-energy photon (gamma ray) from an excited nucleus, which only de-excites the nucleus without changing its atomic number (Z) or mass number (A).
The correct statements are (A), (B), and (D). This corresponds to option (4).

questions.subject: Physics

Choose correct statement/statements :
(a) Nuclear force is independent of charge of nucleons.
(b) Nuclear force has saturation property.
(c) Nuclear force is always Attractive is nature.
(d) Nuclear force exists in range of femtometre.
questions.solution:
- (a) Nuclear force is independent of charge of nucleons. This statement is true. Nuclear forces act equally between proton-proton, neutron-neutron, and proton-neutron pairs.
- (b) Nuclear force has saturation property. This statement is true. A nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbors, not with all other nucleons in the nucleus. This leads to saturation.
- (c) Nuclear force is always Attractive is nature. This statement is false. While predominantly attractive, nuclear forces become strongly repulsive at very short distances (less than about 0.7 fm), preventing the nucleus from collapsing.
- (d) Nuclear force exists in range of femtometre. This statement is true. Nuclear forces are short range forces, effective only over distances of a few femtometers (\(1 \mathrm{fm}=10^{-15} \mathrm{~m}\)).
Therefore, the correct statements are (a), (b), and (d). This corresponds to option (2).

questions.q:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct?
(A) The rest mass of a stable nucleus is less than the sum of the rest masses of its separated nucleons.
(B) The rest mass of a stable nucleus is greater than the sum of the rest masses of its separated nucleons.
(C) In nuclear fusion, energy is released by fusion of two nuclei of medium mass (approx. 100 amu)
(D) In nuclear fusion, energy is released by fragmentation of a very heavy nucleus.
questions.solution:
- (A) The rest mass of a stable nucleus is less than the sum of the rest masses of its separated nucleons. This is the definition of mass defect, which accounts for the binding energy holding the nucleus together. This energy is released when nucleons combine to form a stable nucleus.
- (B) The rest mass of a stable nucleus is greater than the sum of the rest masses of its separated nucleons. This statement is incorrect. If this were true, the nucleus would spontaneously break apart.
- (C) In nuclear fusion, energy is released by fusion of two nuclei of medium mass (approx. 100 amu). This statement is incorrect. Nuclear fusion typically involves the fusion of light nuclei (e.g., hydrogen isotopes) to form heavier, more stable nuclei, releasing energy. Fusion of medium-mass nuclei would generally require energy input rather than releasing it, as their binding energy per nucleon is already high.
- (D) In nuclear fusion, energy is released by fragmentation of a very heavy nucleus. This describes nuclear fission, not fusion. In fission, a heavy nucleus splits into lighter nuclei, releasing energy.

questions.q:
Following statements related to radioactivity are given below:
(A) Radioactivity is a random and spontaneous process and is dependent on physical and chemical conditions.
(B) The number of undecayed nuclei in the radioactive sample decays exponentially with time.
(C) Slope of the graph of \(\log _e(\) no. of undecayed nuclei) vs. time represents the reciprocal of mean life time \((\tau)\).
(D) Product of decay constant \((\lambda)\) and half.-life time \(\left(\frac{T_1}{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\) is not constant.
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Radioactive decay is a random and spontaneous process, it depends on unbalancing of nucleus. This process is dependent on the law of conservation of charge.
We know that, \(N=N_0 e^{-\lambda t} \quad \ldots(1)\), Where, \(N=\) number of decayed nuclei in the sample at time \(t\) and \(N_0=\) initial number of nuclei.
Hence, total number of undecayed nuclei \(N_0-N\)
Thus, \(N_0-N=N_0\left(1-e^{-\lambda t}\right)\)
This shows that the total number of undecayed nuclei decays exponentially with time.
Taking log both sides of equation (1)
\(\ln N=-\lambda t+\ln N_0\)
So, slope \(=-\lambda\) (reciprocal of mean life time)
Half life time \(T_{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}\)
Then, \(\lambda \times T_{\frac{1}{2}}=\ln 2=\mathrm{constant}\)
Hence, (B) and (C) are correct only.

questions.q: Some laws/processes are given in Column I. Match these with the physical phenomena given in Column II and indicate your answer by darkening appropriate bubbles in the $4 \times 4$ matrix given in the ORS.
options: A-p, r; B-p, q, s; C-p; D-q
A-p, r; B-p, q; C-p, r; D-q, s
A-r, s; B-q; C-p; D-p, q, s
questions.solution:
(A) Transition between two atomic energy levels
When an electron in an atom transitions from a higher energy level to a lower one, it emits a photon with a specific energy. This is the fundamental principle behind the emission spectra of elements. The hydrogen spectrum is a classic example of this process, where discrete spectral lines are observed due to transitions between specific energy levels.
- A matches with r.
(B) Electron emission from a material
Electron emission from a material can happen in several ways. One common method is by bombarding the material with photons. If the photons have sufficient energy, they can dislodge electrons from the material's surface. This phenomenon is known as the photoelectric effect.
- B matches with q.
(C) Mosley's law
Moseley's law describes the relationship between the frequency of characteristic X-rays emitted from an element and its atomic number. It states that the square root of the frequency of the emitted X-ray is directly proportional to the atomic number of the element.
- C matches with p.
(D) Change of photon energy into kinetic energy of electrons
This process is the core of the photoelectric effect. A photon with energy \(E=h f\) strikes a material. Some of this energy is used to overcome the work function (\(\phi\)) of the material, and the rest is converted into the kinetic energy of the emitted electron (\(\mathrm{K}_{\text {max }}\)). The equation is \(\mathrm{h} \mathrm{f}= \phi+K_{\text {max }}\).
- D matches with q.
Conclusion
Based on this analysis, the correct pairings are:
- \(\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{r}\)
- \(\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{q}\)
- \(\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{p}\)
- \(\mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{q}\)
This corresponds to option (1). Note that the question has B and D both matching to q, which is a common scenario when both descriptions apply to the same physical phenomenon.

(B) Nuclear Volume(II) Proportional to $A^{1/3}$
(C) Nuclear Density(III) Proportional to $A^1$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
The radius of a nucleus $R$ depends on its mass number $A$ as $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$. Thus, Nuclear Radius is proportional to $A^{1/3}$.

The volume of a nucleus $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$. Thus, Nuclear Volume is proportional to $A^1$.

The nuclear density $\rho = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}} \approx \dfrac{m A}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$. Thus, Nuclear Density is independent of $A$, meaning it is proportional to $A^0$.

The surface area of a nucleus $S = 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi R_0^2 A^{2/3}$. Thus, Nuclear Surface Area is proportional to $A^{2/3}$.

Therefore, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV).

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The density of nuclear matter is approximately constant for all nuclei.
Reason (R): The strong nuclear force is a long-range force and does not show any saturation effect.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
The radius of a nucleus is given by $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$.
The volume of the nucleus is $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A$.
The mass of the nucleus is approximately $mA$, where $m$ is the average mass of a nucleon.
Nuclear density $\rho = \dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Volume}} = \dfrac{mA}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$.
Since $m$ and $R_0$ are constants, the nuclear density is independent of the mass number $A$. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

The strong nuclear force is a short-range force (acting effectively only over distances of a few femtometers) and exhibits a saturation effect, meaning a nucleon interacts strongly only with its nearest neighbours. This saturation is the underlying reason for the constancy of binding energy per nucleon and nuclear density. Thus, Reason (R) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

Answer: $1 \text{ g}$

Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The rest mass of a stable nucleus is always less than the sum of the rest masses of its constituent protons and neutrons.
Reason (R): According to Einstein's mass-energy equivalence, the 'missing' mass is converted into binding energy that is released when the nucleus is broken apart into its constituent nucleons.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion (A) is true: The mass of a stable nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of its constituent nucleons. This difference is known as the mass defect.

Reason (R) is false: When a nucleus is formed from its constituent nucleons, energy is released. Conversely, to break a stable nucleus apart into its constituent free nucleons, energy equal to the binding energy must be supplied to the nucleus, not released.

Therefore, Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

Answer: Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.

Assertion (A): The nuclear density of a heavy nucleus like $^{238}\text{U}$ is approximately the same as that of a light nucleus like $^{4}\text{He}$.

Reason (R): The nuclear force is short-ranged and exhibits the property of saturation, meaning a nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
questions.solution:
The nuclear density is independent of the mass number $A$, meaning all nuclei, whether light like $^{4}\text{He}$ or heavy like $^{238}\text{U}$, have approximately the same nuclear density. Thus, the Assertion is true.

The constancy of nuclear density is a direct consequence of the saturation of nuclear forces. Because the nuclear force is short-ranged, a nucleon only interacts with its nearest neighbours rather than all nucleons in the nucleus. This saturation prevents the nucleus from collapsing into a denser state as more nucleons are added, leading to a constant density and a volume proportional to the mass number. Thus, the Reason is true and correctly explains the Assertion.

Answer: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

The radius of a nucleus is given by $R = R_0 A^{1/3}$.

questions.solution:
In the case of formation of nucleus the evolution of energy equals to the binding energy of the nucleus takes place due to disappearance of a fraction of total mass. If the quantity of mass disappearing is $\Delta m$, then the binding energy is
$B E=\Delta m c^2$
cFrom the above discussion, it is clear that the mass of the nucleus must be less than the sum of the masses of the constituent neutrons and protons. We can then write
$\Delta m=Z m_p-N m_n-m(A, Z)$

options: the electrons present inside the nucleus
the electrons produced as a result of the decay of neutrons inside the nucleus
the electrons produced as a result of collisions between atoms
the electrons orbiting around the nucleus
questions.solution:
Beta decay can involve the emission of either electrons or positrons. The electrons or positrons emitted in a $\beta$-decay do not exist inside the nucleus. They are only created at the time of emission, just as photons are created when an atom makes a transition from higher to a lower energy state.
In negative $\beta$-decay a neutron in the nucleus is transformed into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. Hence, in radioactive decay process, the negatively charged emitted $\beta$-particles are the electrons produced as a result of the decay of neutrons present inside the nucleus.

questions.q: The operation of a nuclear reactor is said to be critical, if the multiplication factor $(k)$ has a value
questions.solution:
The multiplication factor $(k)$ is an important reactor parameter and is the ratio of number of neutrons present at the beginning of a particular generation to the number present at the beginning of the next generation. It is a measure of the growth rate of the neutrons in the reactor. For $k=1$, the operation of the reactor is said to be critical.
Note: If $k$ becomes greater than one, the reaction rate and the reactor power increase exponentially. Unless the factor $k$ is brought down very close to unity, the reactor will become supercritical and can even explode.

questions.solution:
The energy released per nuclear reaction is the resultant binding energy.
Binding energy of $\left({ }_1^2 \mathrm{H}+{ }_1^3 \mathrm{H}\right)=a+b$
Binding energy of ${ }_2^4 \mathrm{He}=c$
In a nuclear reaction the resultant nucleus is more stable than the reactants. Hence, binding energy of ${ }_2^4 \mathrm{He}$ will be more than that of $\left({ }_1^2 \mathrm{H}+{ }_1^3 \mathrm{H}\right)$
Thus, energy released per nucleon
$\begin{aligned}& =\text { resultant binding energy } \\& =c-(a+b)=c-a-b\end{aligned}$
